A 36-year-old female presents to the emergency department with acute onset of unilateral vision loss
that began this evening. She reports no prior similar episodes and is not under regular medical care or
taking any medications. Her history includes occasional self-resolving episodes of weakness and
numbness. Her vital signs show: temperature 99.1°F (36.4°C), blood pressure 101/70 mmHg, pulse
62/min, respirations 19/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination reveals
decreased sensation over the dorsal left foot, and visual examination demonstrates left eye vision loss
with associated eye pain. Which additional clinical finding would most likely be present in this patient?
Answer Choices: (A) Positive Romberg sign (B) Ptosis and diplopia worsening throughout the day (C)
Ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sensation (D) Segmental demyelination on nerve
conduction studies (E) Bilateral spastic paresis of the lower extremities (F) Weakness with repeat
exertion (G) Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (H) Electrical pain with neck flexion
(I) Decreased deep tendon reflexes in the affected limb (J) Hyperreflexia in the lower extremities
 A. Ptosis and diplopia worsening throughout the day
B. Positive Romberg sign
C. Electrical pain with neck flexion
D. Decreased deep tendon reflexes in the affected limb
E. Weakness with repeat exertion
F. Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation
G. Hyperreflexia in the lower extremities
H. Segmental demyelination on nerve conduction studies
I. Bilateral spastic paresis of the lower extremities
J. Ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sensation
